source.title: One Adapter Pair per Model: A Universal Activation Interface for Language Models
source.authors: Su-Hyeon Kim; Jiwan Mun; Yo-Sub Han

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests cross-model representation mapping and tool reuse using a learned shared interface, rather than measuring spontaneous convergence with the original studies’ methods.
record.gate_note: The reported alignment and reuse results are outcomes of an interface trained on matched text, including an explicit contrastive alignment objective; they do not establish that independently trained models naturally converge as they scale. The paper also screens for compatible models before training. State-execution results are not rows for these versions because they measure downstream prediction behavior, not representation similarity. The behavioral-direction PCA is not extracted as a separate row because it is a visualization and its full-space direction cosine is not a measure of the versions’ named input-distance convergence.
record.test_reason: The paper's aim is tool reuse through a trained interface, so most rows report its own method. Its label-free ridge screen (Table 13, App. B.2) is a direct test of V4 in a new setting: a closed-form linear map between native mid-layer LLM activations across nine candidates. The trained-interface translation, probe/NLA reuse and stitching-like execution also bear on V4. Caveat: the interface is trained with a contrastive alignment objective, so its alignment is partly induced on purpose.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct: compatible LLMs can share a frozen activation interface, new models join by fitting only their adapter pair, and probes, a shared SAE and a carrier NLA can be reused. The authors explicitly do not claim this holds for arbitrary model pairs.
record.recipe_differences: The study learns model-wise linear adapters around shared nonlinear modules using matched-prefix self- and cross-reconstruction plus contrastive alignment; onboarding uses matched calibration text. It does not reproduce the original studies’ natural-similarity measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Results differ between ID and OOD retrieval pools. The compatibility screen depends on its reference model and ridge-map procedure; the paper says replacing Llama with Qwen preserves the retained/rejected partition. Onboarding fidelity varies with calibration size, source-model count, and cut depth; the paper reports low seed sensitivity for its tested runs.

fits_no_version.finding: In the trained shared space, behavioral mean-difference directions for the same axis have cosine 0.815 across model pairs, against −0.014 across different axes. All 11 onboarded models match all 9 source axes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Behavioral concept directions coincide across LLMs once mapped into a common space.

record.problems: The main experiment deliberately screens for compatible models, so it does not establish a general result for arbitrary models. Alignment is trained explicitly on matched text rather than measured as an emergent property. OOD exact-match retrieval is much lower than ID retrieval. OLMo has lower round-trip fidelity. Several candidate models fail the preliminary ridge-map screen. The study does not compare alternative similarity metrics or test whether scale or capability independently predicts alignment.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's ten additional model-variant results, SAE reconstruction utility, per-axis NLA classifier recalls, calibration-size and source-count sensitivity values, and front–back execution results were not extracted as rows. They do not directly test the selected convergence or representation-mapping measures, or would exceed the 60-row limit; relevant interpretation is summarized in gate_note and method_sensitivity.

untested.parts: No test of whether alignment of independently trained models rises with size or capability. The screen's passes and failures are not organized by scale, and the onboarded variants are attached to a trained interface.
No same-architecture, different-seed comparison. Seed runs vary only the interface.
Mapping without paired data is not tested. Full-sequence stitching is not tested; only the final-position state is swapped.
The shared SAE is trained on the shared space, so independently learned features recurring across models is not tested.
No comparison of similarity measures or their settings. OOD retrieval is lower, but the authors attribute this to pool difficulty, within a trained interface.
No test of plateaus or of shared data or objectives as the cause.

missing.what: Ridge-map FVE in both directions for all nine candidates: .345–.444 for retained models, mostly negative for rejected ones. This shows large reconstruction loss even where retrieval succeeds.

Front–back execution: translated states consumed by another model's frozen upper layers agree with native B on 72.4–87.7% of next tokens. ΔCE is −0.023 to +0.071 nats, or +0.27–0.38 into OLMo. Relevant to the stitching part of V4.
Ten additional checkpoints (1.24B–14.8B) onboarded with minimum ID R@1 of 99.9–100% and self-FVE of 0.59–0.98.
Replacing the Llama screen reference with Qwen preserves the retained/rejected partition; FVE is more reference-sensitive.

record.verdict_notes: Most rows measure a contrastively trained interface, so the high alignment there is partly by design. The ridge screen is the cleanest test of natural mappability. Its sharply bimodal outcome (≥98.6% vs ≤4.7% R@1) cuts against universal linear interchangeability across LLM families. The screen values were used to select models, so the main results are conditioned on that selection.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test whether independently trained models naturally become more similar as size or capability increases. Scale variants are attached to an explicitly trained interface.
No vision-language paired image and caption alignment is tested.
No same-architecture, different-initialization comparison of learned features or shared subspaces is reported.

The adapters are learned from matched text; the study does not test mapping without paired data. The complete interface includes shared nonlinear modules, so it is not a test of a purely linear map between native representations. It does not test model stitching across full sequences.
A single SAE is trained on shared-space representations. The paper does not test whether independently learned features or circuits recur across models.
No systematic comparison of similarity measures, their settings, or alternative input distributions for the same convergence test is reported.

The compatibility screen reports failures for some candidate models, but the study does not test whether alignment plateaus, compare shared versus different training data or objectives, or establish a causal explanation in terms of a common model of reality.

relationships.condition: Screen-retained models (Qwen3-4B, SmolLM2, Falcon3, OLMo-2 vs Llama-3.2-3B), on retrieval, and the trained interface on in-distribution text
relationships.reason: Ridge linear-map R@1 is 98.6–99.6% (r31–r34). Interface ID R@1 is ≥99.6% (r01–r10). Routed NLA retains 91.6–96.1% of native signal and pooled probes match native probes (r51–r56, r58, r59).
relationships.display_finding: Ridge maps achieved Recall@1 of 98.6–99.6%, the trained interface achieved at least 99.6%, and routed NLA retained 91.6–96.1% of native signal while pooled probes matched native probes.

relationships.condition: Behavioral OOD texts, shared-SAE feature agreement, OLMo NLA routing, and ridge-map reconstruction for retained models
